title: Thermoelectric Cooler Tour
description: Guided walkthrough of a thermoelectric module run as a cooler: a current pumps heat from the block to the sink, Joule heating and conduction work against it, and reversing the current swaps hot and cold.

steps.title: Electricity in, heat moved
steps.body: A current through a thermoelectric module pumps heat from the block on top to the heat sink below. The drive slider sets the current, up to 8 A. Each of the three bodies is coloured by its own temperature from the model: blue below room temperature, red above it.

steps.title: Step 1 — a leg with a temperature profile
steps.body: The module is modelled as one equivalent leg cut into 24 cells between a cold plate and a hot plate. A block sits on the cold plate and a finned sink on the hot one; the sink sheds heat to the 293 K room at 4 W/K. Every cell conducts to its neighbours and is warmed by the current passing through it. The cells settle in a fraction of a second, the block and the sink in tens of seconds — raise Time Dilation to watch them.

steps.title: Step 2 — the junctions pump
steps.body: 127 junction pairs at 0.44 mV/K each give the module S ≈ 0.056 V/K. A current I absorbs heat S·I·T at the cold junction and releases S·I·T at the hot one: about 54 W at 4 A and 242 K. This is the Peltier effect, the Seebeck effect run backwards. The same S makes the module push back with a voltage S·ΔT, which the supply has to overcome on top of I·R.

steps.title: Step 3 — two things work against it
steps.body: The current also heats the leg, I²R in all, and half of that flows back to the cold side. Conduction leaks K·ΔT from hot to cold. What is actually pumped is Q = S·I·T − ½·I²R − K·ΔT. Pumping grows with I and Joule heating with I², so more current stops helping: at 4 A the block reaches about −32 °C, at 8 A only −3 °C, because every extra watt also warms the sink.

steps.title: Step 4 — the load and the COP
steps.body: With nothing to cool, the block is insulated, the pumped heat falls to zero and ΔT across the module can reach at most Z·T²/2 with Z = S²/(R·K) ≈ 0.0025 per kelvin: 76 K here, at about 5.5 A. The load slider feeds heat into the block. At 10 W and 4 A the block sits about 15 K warmer, and the COP — heat pumped over electrical power in — is 0.19. A cooler like this moves one watt of heat for several watts of electricity.

steps.title: Step 5 — reverse the current
steps.body: The current-direction slider flips the sign of I. The junctions swap roles: the block is now heated and the sink side cools. Nothing in the picture is painted hot or cold — the colours follow the temperatures, so they swap too. Keep the current low: with no load path the heated block climbs quickly.

steps.title: What this model is not
steps.body: One equivalent leg stands for all 127 couples, with constant S, R and K; a slope on S, and the Thomson heat that comes with it, exists in the model but is switched off. There is no contact resistance inside the module, no radiation and no frost on the cold plate, and the block loses no heat to the air — the load slider is its only heat source. Temperatures are clamped 150 K below and 250 K above ambient; a real module has failed long before either. It is not a datasheet for any real module and not a cooler or heat-sink design tool.
